texts.exact_text: Shih Ho indicates successful progress (in the condition of things which it supposes). It will be advantageous to use legal constraints.
texts.locator: SBE XVI, Hexagram 21; scan-backed transcription p. 102, hexagram statement
texts.notes: Legge's title restored from the source statement.

texts.exact_text: The first NINE, undivided, shows one with his feet in the stocks and deprived of his toes. There will be no error.
texts.locator: SBE XVI, Hexagram 21; scan-backed transcription p. 102, line 1

texts.exact_text: The second SIX, divided, shows one biting through the soft flesh, and (going on to) bite off the nose. There will be no error.
texts.locator: SBE XVI, Hexagram 21; scan-backed transcription p. 102, line 2

texts.exact_text: The third SIX, divided, shows one gnawing dried flesh, and meeting with what is disagreeable. There will be occasion for some small regret, but no (great) error.
texts.locator: SBE XVI, Hexagram 21; scan-backed transcription p. 102, line 3

texts.exact_text: The fourth NINE, undivided, shows one gnawing the flesh dried on the bone, and getting the pledges of money and arrows. It will be advantageous to him to realise the difficulty of his task and be firm, -- in which case there will be good fortune.
texts.locator: SBE XVI, Hexagram 21; scan-backed transcription p. 102, line 4

texts.exact_text: The fifth SIX, divided, shows one gnawing at dried flesh, and finding the yellow gold. Let him be firm and correct, realising the peril (of his position). There will be no error.
texts.locator: SBE XVI, Hexagram 21; scan-backed transcription p. 102, line 5

texts.exact_text: The sixth NINE, undivided, shows one wearing the cangue, and deprived of his cars. There will be evil.
texts.locator: SBE XVI, Hexagram 21; scan-backed transcription p. 102, line 6

texts.exact_text:
Shih Ho means literally Union by gnawing. We see in the figure two strong lines in the first and last places, while all the others, with the exception of the fourth, are divided. This suggests the idea of the jaws and the mouth between them kept open by something in it. Let that be gnawed through and the mouth will close and the jaws come together. So in the body politic. Remove the obstacles to union, and high and low will come together with a good understanding. And how are those obstacles to be removed? By force, emblemed by the gnawing; that is, by legal constraints. And these are sure to be successful. The auspice of the figure is favourable. There will be success.

Lines 1 and 6 are much out of the game or action described in the figure. Hence they are held to represent parties receiving punishment, while the other lines represent parties inflicting it. The punishment in line 1 is that of the stocks, administered for a small offence, and before crime has made much way. But if the 'depriving' of the toes is not merely keeping them in restraint, but cutting them off, as the Chinese character suggests, the punishment appears to a western reader too severe.

Line 2 is weak, appropriately therefore in an even place, and it is central besides. The action therefore of its subject should be effective; and this is shown by the biting through the soft flesh, an easy thing. Immediately below, however, is a strong offender represented by the strong line, and before he will submit it is necessary to bite off his nose; for punishment is the rule it must be continued and increased till the end is secured.

Line 3 is weak, and in an even place. The action of its subject will be ineffective; and is emblemed by the hard task of gnawing through dried flesh, and encountering, besides, what is distasteful and injurious in it. But again comes in the consideration that here punishment is the rule, and the auspice is not all bad.

Of old, in a civil case, both parties, before they were heard, brought to the court an arrow (or a bundle of arrows), in testimony of their rectitude, after which they were heard; in a criminal case, they in the same way deposited each thirty pounds of gold, or some other metal. See the Official Book of Zhōu. The subject of the fourth line's getting those pledges indicates his exercising his judicial functions; and what he gnaws through indicates their difficulty. Moreover, though the line is strong, it is in an even place; and hence comes the lesson of caution.

The fifth line represents the lord of judgment. As it is a weak line, he will be disposed to leniency; and his judgments will be correct. This is declared by his finding the yellow metal; for yellow is one of the five correct colours. The position is in the centre and that of rule; but the line being weak, a caution is given, as under the previous line.

The action of the figure has passed, and still we have, in the subject of line 6, one persisting in wrong, a strong criminal, wearing the cangue, and deaf to counsel. of course the auspice is evil. 噬嗑 ䷔
texts.locator: SBE XVI, Hexagram 21; scan-backed transcription p. 102, notes

texts.exact_text: 噬嗑：亨。利用獄。
texts.locator: Chinese Wikisource 周易/噬嗑; cross-checked against CTP Book of Changes, hexagram 21, 易經卦辭

texts.exact_text: 頤中有物，曰噬嗑，噬嗑而亨。剛柔分，動而明，雷電合而章。柔得中而上行，雖不當位，利用獄也。
texts.locator: Chinese Wikisource 周易/噬嗑; cross-checked against CTP Book of Changes, hexagram 21, 彖

texts.exact_text: 雷電噬嗑；先王以明罰敕法。
texts.locator: Chinese Wikisource 周易/噬嗑; cross-checked against CTP Book of Changes, hexagram 21, 大象

texts.exact_text: 初九：屨校滅趾，无咎。
texts.locator: Chinese Wikisource 周易/噬嗑; cross-checked against CTP Book of Changes, hexagram 21, 爻 1

texts.exact_text: 屨校滅趾，不行也。

texts.exact_text: 噬膚滅鼻，乘剛也。

texts.exact_text: 六三：噬臘肉，遇毒；小吝，无咎。
texts.locator: Chinese Wikisource 周易/噬嗑; cross-checked against CTP Book of Changes, hexagram 21, 爻 3

texts.locator: Chinese Wikisource 周易/噬嗑; cross-checked against CTP Book of Changes, hexagram 21, 小象 3

texts.exact_text:
The existence of something between the jaws gives rise to the name Shih Ho (Union by means of biting through the intervening article).

The Union by means of biting through the intervening article indicates 'the successful progress (denoted by the hexagram).' The strong and weak (lines) are equally divided (in the figure). Movement is denoted (by the lower trigram ☳), and bright intelligence (by the upper ☲); thunder and lightning uniting in them, and having brilliant manifestation. The weak (fifth) line is in the centre, and acts in its high position. Although it is not in its proper position, this is advantageous for the use of legal constraints.
texts.locator: SBE XVI, Appendix I, Hexagram 21, p. 231

texts.exact_text: (The trigrams ☳ ☲ representing) thunder and lightning form Shih Ho. The ancient kings, in accordance with this, framed their penalties with intelligence, and promulgated their laws.
texts.locator: SBE XVI, Appendix II, Hexagram 21, p. 294

texts.exact_text: 'His feet are in the stocks, and he is deprived of his toes:' -- there is no walking (to do evil).
texts.locator: SBE XVI, Appendix II, Hexagram 21, line 1, p. 294

texts.exact_text: 'He bites through the soft flesh, and (goes on) to bite off the nose:' -- (the subject of the line) is mounted on the strong (first line).
texts.locator: SBE XVI, Appendix II, Hexagram 21, line 2, p. 294

texts.exact_text: 'He meets with what is disagreeable and hurtful:' -- his position is not the proper one for him.
texts.locator: SBE XVI, Appendix II, Hexagram 21, line 3, p. 294

texts.exact_text: 'It will be advantageous to him to realise the difficulty of his task and be firm, in which case there will be good fortune:' -- his light has not yet been sufficiently displayed.
texts.locator: SBE XVI, Appendix II, Hexagram 21, line 4, p. 294

texts.exact_text: 'Let him be firm and correct, realising the peril (of his position), and there will be no error:' -- he will possess every quality appropriate (to his position and task).
texts.locator: SBE XVI, Appendix II, Hexagram 21, line 5, p. 294

texts.exact_text: 'He wears the cangue and is deprived of his ears:' -- he hears, but will not understand.
texts.locator: SBE XVI, Appendix II, Hexagram 21, line 6, p. 294
